title: WhatsApp-style Messaging
problem: Design a 1-to-1 and small group chat system (up to 100 members) with online presence, multi-device sync, and push notifications.
summary: A real-time messaging system for 50M DAU, built around three tiers: (1) stateless API servers for signup/login/profile, (2) stateful chat servers holding long-lived WebSocket connections for real-time send/receive, (3) third-party push-notification integration for offline delivery. Service discovery (ZooKeeper) picks the best chat server for each client at login. Chat history lives in a key-value store (HBase / Cassandra) keyed by channel_id. The dominant design choice is WebSocket for bidirectional traffic (vs HTTP polling or long-polling) — it is the only protocol that lets the server push to the client cheaply over a persistent connection; the main tradeoff is that connection affinity makes rolling deploys and failovers harder than a stateless tier, which is why ZooKeeper coordinates chat-server health and capacity.

functional: 1-to-1 chat and small groups up to 100 members
Real-time delivery to online recipients plus offline push via APNs/FCM
Multi-device sync: same account on phone, laptop, and web see identical history
Delivery and read receipts (sent, delivered, read)
Message history retained forever and searchable
nonFunctional: P99 send-to-receive latency under 500 ms for online recipients
At-least-once delivery with client-side dedupe via message_id
Horizontally scalable to 10M+ concurrent WebSocket connections
Graceful reconnect within 10 s after chat-server failover
End-to-end encryption compatibility (Signal protocol layer above transport)

assumptions: ~60B messages/day across Messenger + WhatsApp (cited Facebook/WhatsApp number)
Max group size: 100 members (book's explicit constraint)
Text messages up to 100,000 chars; no attachments in base design (extension)
Chat history retained forever (book answer to 'how long?')
Per-connection memory ≈ 10 KB → 1M conns ≈ 10 GB on one box (book's sizing exercise)
estimates: Concurrent WebSocket connections at 50M DAU assuming 20% online concurrent ≈ 10M
Chat servers: 10M / 50K per server ≈ 200 chat servers (pre-HA)
Message volume: 50M * 40 msgs/day ≈ 2B msgs/day → ~23K msgs/sec avg, ~70K peak
Message storage (forever): 2B * 200B * 365 ≈ 150 TB/year — requires horizontal KV store
Presence fanout bounded by small-group size (~100 subscribers per user)

client.name: Client (iOS / Android / Web)
client.summary: Opens a persistent WebSocket to a chat server chosen via service discovery; uses HTTP for signup/login/profile. Each device tracks cur_max_message_id for multi-device sync.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- HTTP calls to API servers for signup / login / profile
- Open WSS to the chat server returned by service discovery
- Send heartbeat every ~5s so presence server knows we are online
- ACK received messages; keep `cur_max_message_id` to pull missed messages after reconnect
- Upload media via signed URL (extension beyond text-only base scope)

sections.heading: Multi-device sync (book §Message synchronization)
sections.body: Same user may be logged in on phone AND laptop. Each device keeps `cur_max_message_id`. On reconnect, device fetches messages where `recipient_id == me` AND `message_id > cur_max_message_id` from the KV store.

sections.heading: Reconnect behavior
sections.body: If the chat server drops (crash, deploy), client asks service discovery (ZooKeeper) for a new chat server — book §Error handling. Jittered reconnect prevents thundering herd.

bottlenecks.title: Reconnect thundering herd after chat-server failure
bottlenecks.trigger: When a chat server holding ~50K WebSocket connections crashes or is drained during rolling deploy, all 50K clients simultaneously hit service discovery and reopen WSS. With 200 chat servers at 10M concurrent connections, a single failure = 50K synchronized reconnects; a zone failure could mean millions.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users see 'Connecting…' spinner for 10–60s; message send failures; ZooKeeper and API tier latency spikes; LB SYN backlog overflows; cascading chat-server overload as the herd lands on surviving nodes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Client-side exponential backoff with full jitter (e.g. random wait in [0, min(cap, base * 2^n)], base=1s, cap=30s); stagger initial reconnect by hashing user_id into a 0–10s window; cache last-known chat server and try it first before re-querying ZooKeeper; graceful drain on server side with Connection: close + suggested reconnect-after header.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on reconnect rate > 5x baseline per minute; track p99 time-to-first-message-after-reconnect; monitor ZooKeeper pick_chat_server QPS spikes; dashboard for WS handshake failure ratio > 1%.

bottlenecks.title: Multi-device sync pull storm on reconnect / app foreground
bottlenecks.trigger: On reconnect or wake-from-background, each device issues GET /messages?since=cur_max_message_id. A user active on phone+laptop+web = 3x pulls. After a 12h offline gap in a busy group (hundreds of messages), a single device pulls large ranges from the KV store. At 50M DAU with typical morning wake patterns, this is a correlated 5–10M req/min burst against HBase/Cassandra.
bottlenecks.symptom: First few seconds after opening the app feel laggy; older messages appear progressively; KV store p99 read latency spikes to seconds; users on weak networks see duplicate or out-of-order rendering while catching up.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Paginate pulls (e.g. 50 messages per page, lazy-load on scroll) instead of fetching everything since cur_max_message_id; server-side cap on range size; prefer delta from inbox queue (last N hours) and only hit KV store for deeper history; client-side de-dup by message_id; compress responses (gzip/zstd).
bottlenecks.detection: Track distribution of messages-per-sync-request (alert if p99 > 500); monitor KV store read QPS correlated to regional wake-up hours; measure client-side time-to-interactive after foreground.

bottlenecks.title: Heartbeat traffic overhead at scale
bottlenecks.trigger: Every client sends a heartbeat every 5s. At 10M concurrent connections, this is 2M heartbeat frames/sec across the fleet — ~10K hb/s per chat server (at 50K conns/server), plus forwarding to the presence service. On mobile, 5s heartbeats also prevent radio sleep, draining battery and triggering carrier NAT churn.
bottlenecks.symptom: Elevated mobile battery drain complaints; higher cellular data usage on metered plans; presence service CPU dominated by heartbeat processing; NAT rebinding causing silent WS disconnects between heartbeats.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Adaptive heartbeat interval: 5s on Wi-Fi/foreground, 30–60s on cellular/background; rely on OS-level push (APNs/FCM silent pushes) to wake backgrounded clients instead of app-layer heartbeats; use WebSocket ping frames (2-byte) rather than JSON envelopes; server sets x=30s offline threshold per book, tolerate 2 missed heartbeats.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor heartbeat frames/sec per chat server; track mobile-app battery telemetry (energy impact); alert on presence update churn rate > expected baseline; correlate silent-disconnect rate with NAT timeout windows.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the client is called out as a component In most system designs we treat the client as a dumb terminal, but for WhatsApp-style messaging the client is carrying real state and real logic — enough that it deserves its own box on the diagram. Three things specifically: (1) it holds a **long-lived WebSocket** to a specific chat server, not a fresh HTTP connection each time; (2) it tracks `cur_max_message_id` per device so a user on phone + laptop + web can each independently catch up on what they missed; (3) it sends **heartbeats every ~5s** so the presence service knows whether to show "online" to the user's friends. ## What breaks without a smart client If the client were stateless (just fires HTTP GETs), you lose server-push: the only way to learn about a new message is to poll, which at 50M DAU means constantly hammering the backend for a "no new messages" answer. You'd also lose multi-device sync — opening your laptop after a day away, you'd either re-download everything or miss messages your phone already saw. And without heartbeats, the presence service can't tell "Alice went into a tunnel for 10 seconds" apart from "Alice closed the app." ## The number that forces this design At 50M DAU with ~20% concurrent → **10M live WebSocket connections**. Each one costs ~10 KB of server memory, so 50K conns/server × 200 servers. If every client polled every 5s instead, that's 10M / 5 = **2M requests/sec of mostly-empty polls** — an order of magnitude more load for worse latency. The trade-off: smart clients mean you now ship reconnect logic, backoff, and dedup code to three platforms (iOS, Android, web) and have to keep them compatible with server-side changes forever.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: Fronts both stateless API servers (HTTP) and stateful chat servers (WSS upgrade). Routes HTTP by path, WSS by consistent hash.

sections.heading: Dual role
sections.body: Book groups services into 'stateless' and 'stateful'. The LB sits in front of both: round-robin for stateless API calls, long-lived routing (L4 or sticky L7) for WSS connections to chat servers.

sections.heading: Why L4-ish for chat
sections.body: HTTP/WS upgrades need the LB to get out of the way for the connection's lifetime. L4 pass-through with PROXY protocol preserves client IP at the chat tier.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Chat server dies → ~50K clients reconnect; LB must jitter reconnect storms.
- Rolling deploy drops all connections per host; graceful drain lets clients finish in-flight sends.

lost: Fewer routing knobs than self-hosted HAProxy/Envoy

bottlenecks.title: WebSocket connection table exhaustion at 10M concurrent flows
bottlenecks.trigger: At 50M DAU with ~20% concurrent online, the LB must track ~10M long-lived WSS flows in its connection table. A self-hosted HAProxy/Envoy fleet with the configured concurrency of 200K per instance needs ~50 LB nodes just for WS; a single node hitting its conntrack/file-descriptor limit (default 1M fds, 262K conntrack) silently drops new upgrades.
bottlenecks.symptom: New clients intermittently fail the WSS upgrade with TCP RST or 503; existing connections stay healthy so the issue looks random; `nf_conntrack: table full` in dmesg; LB CPU looks fine but accept queue backs up.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Raise `net.nf_conntrack_max` to 4M+, `fs.file-max` and per-process `ulimit -n` to 2M, `net.core.somaxconn` to 65535; shard WSS across multiple LB pools by user_id hash; or move WS tier to AWS NLB (500K concurrency per node in alternatives, millions of flows/sec) and keep HAProxy only for HTTP API.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB `conntrack_count / conntrack_max > 0.7`; track TCP accept-queue overflow counter (`ListenOverflows`); dashboard WS upgrade success ratio < 99.5% over 1-minute windows.

bottlenecks.title: Reconnect storm overwhelms LB SYN/accept path
bottlenecks.trigger: When a chat server with ~50K WS connections crashes or is drained during rolling deploy, 50K clients reconnect within seconds; a zone-level event can mean 2–3M synchronized SYNs against the LB. The configured 0.0001 failure rate assumes steady-state — reconnect bursts are 10–100x normal accept rate.
bottlenecks.symptom: SYN backlog overflows, clients see `Connecting…` for 10–60s, TLS handshake latency p99 jumps from <10ms to seconds, downstream API tier also slows because login/discovery calls share the LB, cascading to surviving chat servers.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable SYN cookies (`net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1`), bump `tcp_max_syn_backlog` to 65535 and `somaxconn` to 65535; terminate TLS on dedicated LB nodes with session resumption (tickets + 24h cache) so reconnects skip full handshake; coordinate with client-side jittered backoff (0–10s random window) and graceful drain with `Connection: close` + suggested reconnect-after header.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on SYN rate > 5x 1-hour baseline; monitor `ListenDrops` and `TCPReqQFullDoCookies`; track TLS full-handshake ratio (should stay <10% of connections); p99 time-to-WS-established > 500ms.

bottlenecks.title: Rolling LB deploys drop all WSS connections at once
bottlenecks.trigger: An L4 LB holding long-lived WS flows cannot hand off live TCP sockets to a replacement instance. Restarting a single LB node carrying 200K WSS connections forces all of them to reconnect simultaneously, and a full fleet rollout across ~50 LB nodes over an hour means a continuous 50K-100K reconnects/min for the duration.
bottlenecks.symptom: Background reconnect noise during every LB deploy; message send p99 elevated for the deploy window; ZooKeeper `pick_chat_server` QPS doubles; users on flaky mobile networks fail to reconnect and fall back to push notifications.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use LB software that supports hitless reloads (HAProxy `seamless reload` with `-x` socket transfer, Envoy hot restart); schedule deploys during off-peak; drain one LB at a time with long grace (>60s) and advertise via health checks; for managed NLB, rely on provider's transparent target deregistration with connection draining (up to 3600s).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert if WS disconnect rate during a deploy window exceeds 2x baseline; track LB instance uptime histogram vs. connection age distribution; deploy-correlated spike in client reconnect metric.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a load balancer sits in front of WhatsApp For a chat system with 50M daily users, two very different kinds of traffic arrive at the edge: short HTTP calls (login, profile lookups, friend lists) and **long-lived WebSocket connections** that stay open for hours while you chat. The LB is the traffic cop that sorts these: HTTP gets round-robined across any healthy API server, while WebSocket upgrades get pinned to a specific chat server and held open. Without something at the front door, clients would need to know individual server hostnames — which breaks the moment you add, remove, or restart a server. ## What breaks without it If you exposed chat servers directly, a single server crash takes its ~50K users completely offline with no automatic reroute — they'd see "Connecting…" forever because their app has a dead hostname baked in. Operators would see support tickets spike while the other 199 chat servers sit half-idle, because there's no one distributing the reconnect wave across healthy capacity. Rolling deploys become nearly impossible: every restart is a visible outage for whoever was on that box. ## The number that forces it At 20% concurrency, the design expects **~10M simultaneous WebSocket connections** spread across 200 chat servers (10M ÷ 50K per server = 200). The LB has to track all 10M flows and steer new connections toward the least-loaded nodes. That's why the design notes ~50 LB instances at 200K concurrency each (10M ÷ 200K = 50) — the LB tier is itself a scaled-out fleet, not a single box. ## The trade-off Adding an LB means one more hop in every connection and one more tier to operate — but it's the price of being able to add, drain, or lose chat servers without users noticing.

api.name: API Servers (stateless)
api.summary: Stateless HTTP services for signup, login, user profile, friends list, group membership. Book's 'Stateless Services' tier.

sections.heading: Responsibilities (book §Stateless Services)
sections.body:
- POST /signup, POST /login — issue session token
- GET/PUT /users/:id/profile
- GET /users/:id/friends
- Group CRUD (create group, add/remove members)
- On successful login, ask service discovery for the best chat server → return its hostname to client

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: Fully stateless: scale on CPU. Reads hit the user/profile DB (relational). Sessions are token-based (JWT or Redis-backed).

sections.heading: Why separate from chat service
sections.body: Chat servers are stateful (long-lived WS connections). Separating the non-chat surfaces lets us roll / scale API independently and keeps login flows from stalling when chat fleet is under reconnect pressure.

alternatives.name: Monolith (chat + auth + profile in one service)

gained: Fewer moving parts at small scale
lost: Stateful connections block stateless deploys
Can't scale tiers independently — book explicitly argues against this

bottlenecks.title: Login thundering herd against user DB + ZooKeeper after chat-server failure
bottlenecks.trigger: When a chat server with ~50K WS connections dies, clients reconnect; if cached chat-server hostnames are stale or tokens expired, many fall back through /login. A zone-level event can produce 1–3M logins/min, hitting the API tier at ~16–50K QPS vs the per-replica concurrency of 5000. Each login does a bcrypt verify (~50–100ms) plus a userdb SELECT plus a zk.pick_chat_server call.
bottlenecks.symptom: Login p99 climbs from ~20ms to multiple seconds; users stuck on 'Signing in…'; API CPU pinned on bcrypt; user DB connection pool saturated; ZooKeeper pick_chat_server QPS spikes 10x; cascading failures into chat reconnect because clients can't even complete login.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Separate login path from token-refresh path — issue long-lived refresh tokens so reconnects skip bcrypt and DB lookup (hit only a Redis session cache); cache ZooKeeper pick results per-user for 60s; put a token-bucket rate limiter per user_id and per source IP at the API tier (e.g. 5 logins/min/user); scale login replicas independently behind their own pool; use argon2id/bcrypt with tuned cost so verify stays <30ms.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on /login QPS > 3x 1-hour baseline; track bcrypt CPU time as % of request time; monitor userdb connection pool wait time > 50ms; alert on API p99 latency > 200ms for 2 consecutive minutes; dashboard ratio of /login vs /token/refresh calls.

bottlenecks.title: User DB hot-row / hot-shard reads for friends list and group membership
bottlenecks.trigger: GET /users/:id/friends and group membership lookups run on every app foreground and every group send (fanout needs members_of(channel_id)). At 50M DAU with typical 40 opens/day, that's ~23K friends-reads/sec average plus ~23K msgs/sec × avg group size lookups. Viral groups (near the 100-member cap) or celebrity accounts create hot partitions on the sharded-by-user_id relational DB, and cross-shard friend-of-friend joins require app-level fanout.
bottlenecks.symptom: API p99 for profile/friends endpoints creeps to hundreds of ms while p50 stays fine; specific DB shards show 80%+ CPU while others idle; group sends feel slow for large popular groups; connection pool to one shard exhausted.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cache friends list and group_members in Redis with 60–300s TTL and write-through invalidation on membership change (read-through cache absorbs the 23K QPS); for group_members, cache keyed by channel_id at the chat tier so sends don't round-trip through API+DB; use read replicas for profile reads; consider denormalizing member list into the channel record to avoid the join.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard CPU and QPS dashboards with alert on shard CPU > 70% or QPS skew > 3x mean; cache hit ratio on friends/members caches (alert if < 90%); p99 latency per endpoint broken down by shard id; slow query log for SELECTs > 50ms.

bottlenecks.title: Session token validation overhead on every API call
bottlenecks.trigger: Every authenticated API call (profile fetch, friends list, group CRUD, signed-URL request for media) revalidates the session token. If sessions are Redis-backed, that's 1 Redis GET per request; at peak API load across a 50M DAU fleet this adds up to tens of thousands of Redis GETs/sec in addition to the actual work. If JWTs are used, signature verification adds CPU per request and revocation requires a denylist lookup anyway.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis session store becomes a shared dependency for every API replica; a Redis blip shows up as elevated API latency across every endpoint simultaneously; API CPU includes non-trivial JWT verify cost; logout/revocation latency unclear to users.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use short-lived JWTs (5–15 min) with asymmetric signing verified in-process (no network hop) + a refresh-token flow hitting Redis only on refresh; cache JWT verify results per-connection in API worker memory; keep a small bloom-filter denylist for revoked tokens in-process, synced every 30s.
bottlenecks.detection: Track auth middleware time as % of total request time (target <5%); Redis session GET QPS and p99; alert on auth-layer error rate > 0.1%; monitor ratio of refresh vs new-login calls to confirm refresh path is doing its job.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why stateless API servers sit alongside the chat tier WhatsApp-style messaging has two completely different kinds of work. One kind is *real-time* — your open chat window, messages flying back and forth — and that needs a persistent WebSocket connection to a specific chat server that remembers you. The other kind is *everything else*: signing up, logging in, updating your profile photo, creating a group, adding a friend. These are one-shot HTTP requests where any server can answer. Mixing them into the chat tier would be a disaster, because chat servers are *stateful* (they hold 50K live WebSocket connections each) and can't be restarted or scaled freely. The API tier exists to keep the boring-but-critical account stuff on machines you can reboot whenever you want. ## What breaks without it Imagine the chat servers also handled login. During a rolling deploy — which happens weekly — every restart kicks 50K users offline *and* blocks new users from logging in, because the login code is on the same box being restarted. Operators would see login success rate tank every deploy; users would see "can't sign in" errors that mysteriously clear up 10 minutes later. ## The number At 50M DAU, users log in, fetch friends lists, and open profiles constantly — easily 100K+ HTTP requests/sec across the fleet, totally separate from the ~23K messages/sec going through chat servers. Scaling on CPU, a single API replica handles ~5K concurrent requests, so you need ~20+ API replicas — and critically, you can add or remove them in seconds without disturbing a single WebSocket. ## The trade-off Two tiers means two deploy pipelines and one extra network hop on login, in exchange for being able to scale and restart each tier on its own schedule.

zk.name: Service Discovery (ZooKeeper)
zk.summary: Registers all chat servers and picks the best one for each client at login based on geo, load, and health.

sections.heading: Role (book §Service discovery)
sections.body: Book explicitly names Apache ZooKeeper. Primary job: 'give the client a list of DNS host names of chat servers that the client could connect to.' Picks best server by geographic location, server capacity, etc.

sections.heading: Login flow (book Figure 12-11)
sections.body:
1. Client hits API with credentials
2. API authenticates against user DB
3. API asks ZooKeeper: which chat server should user X connect to?
4. ZooKeeper picks (e.g. chat-server-2) based on load/geo
5. API returns that hostname
6. Client opens WebSocket to chat-server-2

sections.heading: Error handling (book §Error handling)
sections.body: If a chat server goes offline, its ephemeral znode is reaped. Clients reconnect and ZooKeeper hands them a different live server — chat recovery without a manual failover dance.

lost: Smaller ecosystem of client libs for service registration patterns

gained: Built-in health checking and DNS interface
lost: More components to run than pure ZooKeeper/etcd

bottlenecks.title: pick_chat_server QPS spike during reconnect storms
bottlenecks.trigger: A chat server holding ~50K WebSocket connections crashes or is drained during rolling deploy; all 50K clients simultaneously re-login and hit ZooKeeper for a new server assignment. A zone-level event across ~70 chat servers (1/3 of 200) = ~3.5M pick_chat_server calls in under a minute, far exceeding the configured 5000 concurrency per ZK node.
bottlenecks.symptom: Login p99 jumps from ~10ms to seconds; ZooKeeper request queue backs up; API tier threads block waiting on pick_chat_server; users see 'Connecting…' for 30–60s; surviving chat servers get lopsided load because assignments are made with stale capacity data.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Put a 60s read-through cache of pick results in the API tier (keyed by user_id) so retries skip ZK; serve pick_chat_server from ZK observers/followers (read-only replicas) rather than the leader; pre-compute a ranked chat-server list per geo refreshed every 5s instead of scoring on each request; client-side jittered backoff (0–10s) to flatten the herd before it reaches ZK.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on pick_chat_server QPS > 3x 1-hour baseline; ZK request latency p99 > 100ms; ZK outstanding_requests metric > 1000; watch JMX NumAliveConnections and OutstandingRequests on each ensemble node.

bottlenecks.title: Ephemeral znode churn from chat-server heartbeats
bottlenecks.trigger: Each of 200 chat servers maintains an ephemeral znode with session heartbeats (tickTime typically 2s). Any session timeout (network blip, GC pause > tickTime*2) deletes the znode and forces watchers on all API servers to re-fire. During a network partition or a full chat-tier rolling deploy, dozens of znodes flap per minute, triggering watch-fanout storms to every API replica that cached a chat-server list.
bottlenecks.symptom: API servers briefly see empty or stale chat-server lists and route new logins to dead or decommissioning servers; ZK leader CPU spikes from watch notification fanout; zxid advances rapidly; transient 'no chat server available' errors on login even though capacity exists.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tune ZK tickTime to 4s and session timeout to 20–40s so transient GC/network blips don't reap znodes; use a dedicated watcher-aggregator service that subscribes once and exposes a cached view to API replicas (instead of every API server watching directly); quarantine flapping servers with a 30s cooldown before re-advertising them as pickable.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ephemeral-node create/delete rate > 10/min cluster-wide; monitor ZK watch_count and fsync latency; track znode session expiration events in ZK logs; dashboard for gap between 'chat servers registered in ZK' and 'chat servers passing LB health check'.

bottlenecks.title: ZooKeeper write-leader bottleneck limits cluster elasticity
bottlenecks.trigger: ZooKeeper serializes all writes through a single leader; ephemeral znode creation, session heartbeat renewals, and load/capacity metadata updates (if stored in ZK) all land on one node. With 200 chat servers each updating capacity every few seconds plus the presence-related registrations, write throughput is capped at a few thousand ops/sec regardless of ensemble size — adding more ZK nodes only helps reads.
bottlenecks.symptom: When operators try to push fine-grained load data into ZK (so pick_chat_server ranks accurately), write latency climbs into hundreds of ms; fsync time on the leader's transaction log becomes the critical path; scaling chat fleet past 200 nodes shows diminishing returns.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Keep only coarse registration/health in ZK; store fast-changing load/capacity metrics out-of-band (Redis, gossip, or a periodic pull from chat servers); put ZK's dataDir and dataLogDir on dedicated NVMe with separate disks for snapshot and txn log; consider migrating to etcd (listed as alternative) for simpler Raft ops, or a two-tier model where ZK holds membership and a secondary cache holds load.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor ZK leader fsync_time_ms p99 (alert > 50ms); track outstanding proposals and commit latency; alert if write QPS approaches 70% of measured ensemble ceiling; watch for leader elections (any election > 1/day is a red flag).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why ZooKeeper sits in this design The chat tier is **stateful** — once Alice's phone opens a WebSocket to `chat-server-2`, that specific box holds her connection in memory for hours. But which of the ~200 chat servers should her phone connect to in the first place? It can't be random (some are overloaded, some are in the wrong region, some are about to be drained for a deploy), and it can't be baked into the app (servers come and go constantly). ZooKeeper is the live registry that answers the question "which chat server should this user use *right now*?" every time someone logs in or reconnects. ## What happens without it If the API tier just round-robined users onto chat servers, a crashed or draining server would keep receiving new connections for minutes until DNS or health checks caught up — users would see "Connecting…" spinners, and operators would see a pile of failed WebSocket upgrades on a zombie node while healthy servers sat half-empty. Worse, during the daily rolling deploy, there'd be no coordinated way to stop sending new users to a server that's about to restart. ## The number At 50M DAU with 20% concurrency, that's **10M live WebSocket connections across ~200 chat servers** (10M ÷ 50K per server). Every login — and every reconnect after a crash — makes one `pick_chat_server` call. A single chat-server failure releases 50K clients that all re-query ZooKeeper within seconds, so the registry has to be both authoritative *and* fast to read. ## The trade-off Introducing ZooKeeper adds one more critical dependency on the login path, in exchange for being able to add, remove, and fail chat servers without the clients ever needing to know their hostnames.

chat.name: Chat Servers (stateful WebSocket)
chat.summary: Stateful WebSocket servers holding persistent connections. Book's only 'Stateful Service' — each client stays on one chat server as long as it is available.

sections.heading: Why WebSocket (book §Polling/LongPolling/WebSocket)
sections.body:
The book walks through three protocols:
- **Polling**: client asks periodically — wastes server resources, mostly returns empty.
- **Long polling**: holds connection open until message arrives — stateless LBs can land sender and receiver on different servers; no good disconnect detection; still periodic after timeouts.
- **WebSocket**: bidirectional, persistent, upgrades over ports 80/443 so it works through firewalls. Used for BOTH send and receive — simplifies design. This is what the book recommends.

sections.heading: Per-connection state
sections.body: User id, device id, last seen seq, heartbeat timer, pending ACK map. Kept in-process (stateful). Stickiness comes from ZooKeeper telling the client which chat server to use.

sections.heading: Send path (book 1-on-1 Figure 12-12)
sections.body:
1. Receive message from User A's WebSocket
2. Obtain msg_id from the ID generator (Snowflake OR local per-channel counter)
3. Publish to the message sync queue (recipient's inbox)
4. Queue writer persists to KV store
5. If User B is online, forwarded to User B's chat server via the queue; else push-notification server wakes B
6. User B's chat server forwards to User B over its WebSocket

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: ~50K connections/node. At 50M DAU and 20% concurrent online → ~10M / 50K = 200 chat servers. Restart drains connections over ~60s; ZooKeeper reroutes new connections.

gained: Works everywhere HTTP works, no protocol upgrade
lost: Sender and receiver may hit different servers (stateless LB)
Server can't tell if client is disconnected
Wastes traffic when user is idle
Book: 'could be costly… consume precious server resources to answer a question that offers no as an answer most of the time'
XML framing is heavier than protobuf
Lower per-node connection density
Pub/sub topic model is awkward for 1:1 chat semantics

bottlenecks.title: Connection capacity cliff at 50K WebSockets per node
bottlenecks.trigger: Each chat server targets ~50K concurrent WS connections at ~10KB/conn (≈500MB just for socket buffers, plus per-conn app state: user_id, device_id, pending ACK map, heartbeat timers). At 10M concurrent connections across 200 nodes, losing even 10 nodes (zone blip, bad deploy) forces the surviving 190 to absorb +26K conns each, pushing them past 75K — beyond the file-descriptor, epoll, and memory budget the node was sized for.
bottlenecks.symptom: WS upgrades start failing with 503 or TCP RST on survivors; existing connections get evicted by OOM killer or slow GC pauses; send-path p99 jumps from ~10ms to seconds; cascading failure as evicted clients reconnect and overload the next node.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Hard cap accepted connections per node at 55K with early 503 + Retry-After so ZooKeeper reroutes; tune ulimit -n to 200K, net.core.somaxconn=65535, use epoll/kqueue with edge-triggered IO; run WS tier on a language/runtime with cheap fibers (Go, Elixir, Rust tokio) rather than thread-per-conn; keep 30% headroom in fleet sizing (260 nodes not 200) so N-2 zone loss is survivable; pre-allocate buffers and avoid per-message heap allocation to keep 10KB/conn budget real.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-node gauges: active_ws_connections, fd_usage_ratio, rss_bytes; alert when any node > 80% of cap or fleet p95 > 70%; track WS upgrade success ratio < 99.5% over 1-min; memory growth slope per connection (catch leaks before cap).

bottlenecks.title: Stateful stickiness blocks rolling deploys and failover
bottlenecks.trigger: Unlike the stateless API tier, chat servers hold long-lived WS connections that cannot be hot-migrated. A rolling deploy of all 200 nodes at 50K conns each = 10M forced reconnects over the deploy window; a single node restart = 50K synchronized reconnects in seconds. Any in-flight SEND with an unacknowledged msg_id risks loss or duplicate delivery if the inbox-queue produce hasn't committed.
bottlenecks.symptom: Every deploy produces a visible latency spike and 'Connecting…' spinners for affected users; ZooKeeper pick_chat_server QPS spikes 50–100x; surviving nodes get lopsided load from herd landing; support tickets for 'missed messages' or 'duplicate sends' during deploy windows.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Graceful drain protocol: stop accepting new WS, send CLOSE with suggested-reconnect-after jitter (0–30s) spread across the 50K conns, wait for in-flight SEND→queue acks before exit (target <60s drain); enforce exactly-once by idempotent produce keyed on client_msg_id so retries dedupe at queue consumer; deploy at most 1–2 nodes concurrently out of 200 with 2-min pauses; client prefers last-known server on reconnect before re-querying ZK to smooth the herd.
bottlenecks.detection: Deploy-window SLO: WS reconnect rate < 3x baseline and no more than 1% of users see >5s disconnect; track per-deploy distribution of drain duration and un-ACKed SEND count at shutdown; alert on duplicate msg_id rate at consumer > 0.01%.

bottlenecks.title: Group fanout amplification at send time
bottlenecks.trigger: For a 100-member group (design's max), a single SEND on a chat server triggers: 1 idgen call + 1 group_members lookup + 99 queue produces + 99 presence checks, inflating per-message work ~100x. At 70K peak msgs/sec mixed with busy groups, a handful of active 100-member channels can consume a disproportionate share of a node's CPU and queue-producer throughput, starving 1:1 sends on the same node.
bottlenecks.symptom: 1:1 message p99 latency on a given chat server correlates with which groups happen to be active there; queue producer backpressure (Kafka buffer full) on some nodes but not others; presence service QPS spikes per burst of group activity; uneven CPU across nodes despite even connection count.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Batch queue produces: one produceBatch call with 99 records instead of 99 individual calls (Kafka linger.ms=5, batch.size=64KB); cache group_members (keyed by channel_id, TTL 60s, invalidate on membership change) so fanout skips the userdb hop; batch presence lookups (MGET for all 99 recipients in one call); rate-limit per-channel send QPS at the chat server to prevent one spammy group saturating a node; consider moving group fanout to a dedicated fanout worker consuming a 'raw-send' topic, decoupling from the WS event loop.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-send work amplification metric (queue_produces_per_send, presence_lookups_per_send) broken down by channel_id; alert if p99 > 120 or mean > 20; CPU-per-message histogram; Kafka producer buffer-full rate per chat server node > 1/min.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why chat servers exist in WhatsApp The whole point of a messaging app is that when Alice types "hello," Bob's phone lights up *immediately* — not 5 seconds later when his phone next polls a server. That "push from server to client" is the hard part, and it's what the chat servers exist to do. They hold a **persistent WebSocket** open to every online device, so the server can shove a message down the pipe the instant it arrives. The API tier can't do this job: API servers are stateless and treat each HTTP request independently, but a WebSocket is a long-lived connection that must stay pinned to one specific server for hours. ## What happens without them If you tried to do this with plain HTTP, every client would have to poll ("any new messages? any new messages?") every couple of seconds. At 10M concurrent users polling every 5s, that's **2M requests/sec of mostly-empty responses** hammering your backend — an order of magnitude more load than the actual message traffic, for a *worse* user experience (up to 5s delay on every message). Operators would see their database melt from pointless reads; users would see laggy chats and dead battery life. ## The number The design expects 50M DAU × 20% concurrent = **10M live WebSocket connections**. At ~10KB of memory per connection and ~50K connections per server, that's 10M ÷ 50K = **200 chat servers**, each holding ~500MB of socket state. One machine couldn't possibly do this — fanning out across a dedicated stateful tier is the only way the math works. ## The trade-off Stateful servers make deploys and failures painful (restarting one box kicks 50K users offline), but that pain is the price of true real-time delivery.

idgen.name: Message ID Generator
idgen.summary: Produces unique, time-sortable message_ids. Book considers three options: auto_increment, Snowflake (global), local per-channel sequence.

sections.heading: Requirements (book §Message ID)
sections.body: message_id must be: (1) unique, (2) sortable by time — new rows have higher IDs than old ones. Used as partition-clustering key in the KV store.

sections.heading: Recommended approach
sections.body: Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs (timestamp | machine | seq). Book references Chapter 7. Generated in-process on the chat server that owns the send — no extra hop.

sections.heading: Alternative: local sequence per channel
sections.body: Book notes this is 'easier to implement than the global ID implementation' because maintaining order within a single 1:1 or group channel is sufficient — you don't need global ordering.

sections.heading: Why not DB auto-increment
sections.body: Book: 'NoSQL databases usually do not provide such a feature' — and the KV store we chose for history does not have it.

lost: Not globally unique across channels
Need per-channel atomic counter (e.g. Redis INCR keyed by channel_id)
Not available in NoSQL KV store
Single primary caps write throughput

bottlenecks.title: Clock skew / NTP jumps break Snowflake monotonicity
bottlenecks.trigger: Snowflake packs timestamp_ms in the high 41 bits; if a chat server's clock steps backwards (NTP correction, VM pause, leap-second handling) even by a few ms, newly issued IDs fall below previously issued ones. With 200 chat servers each running an in-process generator at ~70K peak msgs/sec, the probability of at least one clock anomaly per day is high.
bottlenecks.symptom: Messages appear out of order in a channel; KV store clustering key (message_id within channel_id) no longer reflects send order; multi-device sync using `message_id > cur_max_message_id` silently skips messages issued during the backward jump; duplicate message_ids possible if seq counter also resets.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Refuse to issue IDs when `now_ms < last_issued_ms` — either sleep until time catches up (if drift <10ms) or fail fast and fall back to a peer generator; run chrony with `makestep` disabled and slew-only corrections; monotonic-clock-based timestamp source rather than wall clock; reserve extra seq bits (e.g. 14 instead of 12) so bursts within the same ms don't overflow after a pause.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-generator metric for `backward_clock_events` (alert on any); monitor `issued_id < last_issued_id` guard-trips; alert on NTP offset > 5ms on any chat server; dashboard histogram of inter-ID timestamp deltas per server.

bottlenecks.title: Per-ms sequence overflow under peak burst
bottlenecks.trigger: Snowflake's 12-bit seq allows 4096 IDs per machine per ms = ~4M IDs/sec per generator. At 70K peak msgs/sec fleet-wide this is fine on average, but group fanout-on-write amplifies: a single send to a 100-member group produces 1 msg_id call (not 100) — however, if local-sequence-per-channel alternative is chosen and a viral channel receives a burst, or if multiple chat servers share a machine_id due to misconfiguration, the 4096/ms ceiling is reachable.
bottlenecks.symptom: ID generator stalls (spin-waits for next ms) causing send-path p99 latency spikes from ~5ms to tens of ms; in worst case seq wraps and issues a duplicate message_id, violating KV primary key and causing INSERT failures or silent overwrites; SEND ACKs delayed and clients retry, producing duplicates at the queue layer.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Ensure machine_id is globally unique (assign via ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential znode at chat-server startup, not config file); widen seq to 14 bits (16K/ms) by borrowing from machine_id bits since 200 servers only need 8 bits; on seq exhaustion, spin-wait to next ms rather than wrap; add a hard assertion that issued_id > last_issued_id before returning.
bottlenecks.detection: Counter for `seq_exhaustion_waits_per_sec` (alert > 100/s per server); p99 latency of `idgen.next` (alert > 2ms); duplicate-key errors on KV store INSERT; audit distinct machine_id values against expected fleet size.

bottlenecks.title: Machine-id collision on chat-server restart / autoscale
bottlenecks.trigger: Snowflake's 10-bit machine_id field supports 1024 distinct servers — comfortable for the current 200 chat-server fleet, but during a rolling deploy or autoscale event a restarted node can re-register before ZooKeeper reaps its old ephemeral znode (session timeout 20–40s), allowing two processes to claim the same machine_id for a brief window. Both will emit IDs with identical (timestamp, machine_id, seq) tuples.
bottlenecks.symptom: Rare duplicate message_ids across the fleet; KV store INSERTs silently overwrite or hit primary-key conflicts; clients see message A replaced by message B in history after a reconnect pulls from KV; impossible-to-reproduce bugs clustered around deploy windows.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Allocate machine_id via ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential znode with a short session timeout and `wait-for-reap` guard on startup (refuse to emit IDs until previous znode for the same slot is gone); embed a 4-bit epoch/generation counter in the ID (reducing seq or machine_id bits) that increments on each process start; alternatively, use (pod_uid_hash mod 1024) only after verifying uniqueness against live registry.
bottlenecks.detection: ZooKeeper audit: alert on any two live chat-server znodes advertising the same machine_id; periodic scan of KV store for duplicate message_id within a time window; startup log line `acquired machine_id=X` counted and cross-checked; canary query `SELECT message_id, COUNT(*) FROM messages_1on1... HAVING COUNT(*)>1`.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a dedicated ID generator for WhatsApp-style chat Every message in this system needs an ID that does two jobs at once: it has to be **unique** across the whole fleet (so Alice's "hello" doesn't collide with Bob's "hi" stored on the same KV partition), and it has to be **time-sortable** (so when Bob's phone loads a chat, messages appear in the order they were sent). The KV store uses `message_id` as the clustering key inside a channel — that's literally how history is ordered on disk. You can't use `created_at` timestamps because two messages can easily share the same millisecond, and you can't use the database's auto-increment because HBase/Cassandra don't offer one. So something has to mint these IDs, and that something is the ID generator. ## What happens without it If message IDs were just random UUIDs, the KV store would still work — but a chat window would show messages in random order because the clustering key wouldn't reflect send time. Users would see "hello" appear *after* "how are you?" If IDs instead came from per-server counters with no coordination, two chat servers could issue the same ID for different messages, and one would silently overwrite the other in the KV store. Users would complain their messages "disappeared"; operators would see nothing in the logs. ## The number At peak the system handles **~70K messages/sec**, and a 64-bit Snowflake ID with timestamp-in-the-high-bits can produce 4,096 IDs per millisecond per machine — that's 4M/sec per generator, so even one generator per chat server (200 servers) has ~11,000× headroom over the 70K/sec peak. ## Trade-off Snowflake IDs are cheap and decentralized, but they depend on reasonably synchronized clocks — a server whose clock jumps backwards can issue IDs that break the sort order.

presence.name: Presence Servers
presence.summary: Manages online/offline status via client heartbeats; fans out status changes to friends through per-pair pub/sub channels.

sections.heading: Heartbeat (book §User disconnection)
sections.body: Client sends heartbeat every ~5s. If presence server receives no heartbeat within x seconds (book uses x=30), user is marked offline. This avoids flapping when a user briefly loses signal (e.g. tunnel).

sections.heading: Storage
sections.body: Presence state in KV store: `user_id → {status, last_active_at}`. TTL on the key reaps zombies after a crash.

sections.heading: Online status fanout (book §Online status fanout, Figure 12-19)
sections.body: Pub/sub per friend pair — channel `A-B` is subscribed by B, published by A. When A's status changes, it publishes to all pair-channels (A-B, A-C, A-D). Bounded fanout for small friend lists.

sections.heading: Limit at large scale
sections.body: Book: for a group of 100,000 people, 1 status change = 100K events → too expensive. Workaround: fetch status on demand (when user opens the chat / refreshes friend list) rather than pushing.

gained: Book's recommendation for huge friend lists — avoids N^2 fanout
lost: Stale: friend shows 'online' even after they closed the app until you refresh
Presence can lag ~1-2s
More complex to reason about

bottlenecks.title: Heartbeat ingestion overload at 2M hb/sec fleet-wide
bottlenecks.trigger: Every one of ~10M concurrent clients sends a heartbeat every 5s = 2M heartbeats/sec into the presence tier. At the configured 10K concurrency per presence replica, this requires ~200 replicas just for steady-state heartbeat absorption, and any replica loss or GC pause instantly backs up heartbeat queues since every client retries within 5s.
bottlenecks.symptom: Presence service CPU pinned at >80% doing heartbeat bookkeeping; last_active_at updates lag by seconds to minutes; users briefly flip to 'offline' then back to 'online' (flapping) because heartbeats arrive after the 30s timeout; KV store write QPS dominated by presence TTL refreshes rather than actual status changes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Adaptive heartbeat intervals (5s foreground/Wi-Fi, 30–60s background/cellular) to cut baseline load 6–12x; aggregate heartbeats at the chat server — one chat server holds 50K conns and can batch-forward a single 'still-alive bitmap' every 5s instead of 50K individual calls, cutting presence ingress from 2M/s to ~200/s (one per chat server); store last_active_at in Redis with EXPIRE=30s rather than a full KV write per heartbeat.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on presence ingress QPS > 3x expected baseline (expected = chat_server_count / 5s if aggregated, or DAU*0.2/5 if not); monitor presence replica CPU > 70%; track p99 heartbeat-to-last_active_at propagation delay (alert > 2s); dashboard for status flap rate (online→offline→online within 60s) > 0.1% of users.

bottlenecks.title: Pub/sub fanout explosion for users with large friend lists
bottlenecks.trigger: Per the book's per-pair channel model, a status change for a user with F friends publishes F events. Average friend count ~200 is manageable (200 events/change), but power users with 1000+ friends generate 1000 events per online/offline transition. At 50M DAU with typical app-open/close churn of ~10 status changes per user per day, average fanout is ~100K events/sec, and heavy-tail users can burst 10K+ events from a single app switch.
bottlenecks.symptom: Presence pub/sub backlog grows during morning/evening app-open waves; friends of power users see stale online indicators for tens of seconds; presence CPU spikes correlate with specific user_ids; chat servers subscribed to many pair-channels see elevated event-processing latency that bleeds into WS send latency.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Book's recommended fallback: switch to on-demand/pull presence for users with friend_count > threshold (e.g. 500) — only fetch status when the user actually opens a chat or refreshes friend list; coalesce rapid status flips into a single event with a 2–5s debounce (avoids flap amplification); shard pub/sub channels by user_id hash so hot publishers don't saturate a single broker partition; use Redis pub/sub or NATS with per-subscriber filtering rather than per-pair channels when F is large.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram of fanout-events-per-status-change (alert if p99 > 1000); per-user event emission rate (top-N dashboard to catch celebrity accounts); pub/sub broker backlog depth per partition; time-from-status-change-to-friend-notification p99 > 3s.

bottlenecks.title: Presence state lookup hot path on every group send
bottlenecks.trigger: The 1:1 and group send flows both call presence.get(recipient_id) to decide whether to push over WS or route to the notification service. At 70K peak msgs/sec with group fanout up to 100 members, worst-case presence lookups = 70K × 100 = 7M/sec — well beyond the configured 10K concurrency per replica, and far higher than the heartbeat ingress.
bottlenecks.symptom: Send-path p99 latency becomes correlated with presence service health; presence read QPS dwarfs heartbeat QPS; cache misses during presence replica restarts cause send latency spikes; in pathological cases, message delivery stalls waiting for presence lookups, triggering client-side retries and duplicate sends.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cache presence at the chat server with 5–10s TTL (staleness tolerable — worst case is one unnecessary push notification); batch presence lookups for group sends into a single MGET call (100 members → 1 request, not 100); co-locate presence data in Redis Cluster sharded by user_id so chat servers can read directly without going through a presence-service RPC hop; for group fanout, fetch all member statuses once and reuse across the N queue produces.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-send presence_lookups_per_message metric (alert if mean > 10 after caching); presence service read QPS vs write QPS ratio (alert if read > 100x write, indicating missing cache); chat-server-side presence cache hit ratio < 95%; correlation between presence p99 and send-path p99 on dashboards.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why presence servers exist in WhatsApp The problem statement explicitly calls out "online presence" as a feature — that little green dot next to a friend's name, or the "last seen 5 minutes ago" text. Someone has to be the authoritative answer to "is Alice online right now?" and it can't be the chat servers alone, because Alice might be connected to `chat-server-2` while Bob (who wants to see her status) is on `chat-server-7`. The presence service is the shared source of truth that every chat server can consult, plus the thing that pushes status *changes* out to friends so their UI updates without refreshing. ## What breaks without it If you ripped presence out, the green dot would either disappear entirely or go stale — Alice closes the app, but Bob's phone still shows her as "online" for hours. Worse, the send path uses presence to decide whether to push a message over WebSocket or route it through APNs/FCM. Without presence, every message would have to *try* the WebSocket first and fall back on timeout, adding seconds of latency, or you'd send redundant push notifications to users already reading in-app. ## The number At 50M DAU with 20% concurrency, ~10M clients each send a heartbeat every 5s — that's **2M heartbeats/sec** just to keep presence fresh. And a status flip for a user with 200 friends means publishing 200 fanout events, so even modest app-open/close churn generates ~100K fanout events/sec fleet-wide. This volume is why presence is a dedicated tier, not a column in the user DB. ## Trade-off Real-time presence costs continuous heartbeat traffic and battery drain; the book accepts that cost in exchange for a UX where "online" actually means online.

queue.name: Message Sync Queue
queue.summary: Per-recipient inbox. Chat server publishes one copy of the message per recipient; each recipient's chat server (or notifier) consumes from it.

sections.heading: Role (book §1-on-1 chat flow, §Small group chat flow)
sections.body: Book: 'You can think of the message sync queue as an inbox for a recipient.' In group chat with N members, the sender's chat server writes N copies — one to each member's inbox. Simplifies receive logic: each client only reads its own inbox.

sections.heading: Why N copies for small groups
sections.body: Book: 'When the group number is small, storing a copy in each recipient's inbox is not too expensive.' WeChat uses this approach up to 500 members. At very large group size, fanout cost dominates and a different model is needed.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.body: Kafka-style partitioned log is a good fit: partition by recipient_id so each recipient's inbox is an ordered stream. Producer acks=all; consumers are chat servers + persistence writer + notification service (separate consumer groups).

gained: Saves storage for huge groups (no N copies)
lost: Every read does a group-membership join
Doesn't match book's recommended small-group model
Smaller ecosystem than Kafka

bottlenecks.title: Group fanout write amplification saturates partitions
bottlenecks.trigger: Per-recipient fanout-on-write means a single send to a 100-member group (design's max) produces 99 queue records. At 70K peak msgs/sec fleet-wide, if even 10% of traffic is group sends averaging 50 members, that's ~350K produces/sec just from fanout, on top of ~63K 1:1 produces — total ~410K produces/sec. Hot channels (active large groups) concentrate onto single partitions keyed by recipient_id, creating skewed load.
bottlenecks.symptom: Kafka producer buffer-full errors on chat servers; producer p99 latency climbs from <10ms to hundreds of ms; send-path ACK latency degrades for both 1:1 and group; specific broker partitions show >80% disk/CPU while others idle; consumer lag spikes on popular users' inbox partitions.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use producer batching aggressively (linger.ms=5-10, batch.size=64KB, compression=lz4) so 99 fanout records coalesce into 1-2 network round-trips; over-partition the inbox topic (e.g. 1024 partitions) so recipient_id hash spreads hot users; increase producer buffer.memory to 128MB per chat server; set acks=1 (not all) for fanout copies since KV store is the durable record, or use a separate lower-durability topic for fanout with acks=all only on the persistence topic.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Kafka producer record-send-rate > 3x baseline or buffer-available-bytes < 20%; per-partition bytes-in-per-sec skew (alert if max/mean > 5x); produce p99 > 50ms; consumer-lag per partition with alert on any partition lag > 10K records.

bottlenecks.title: Multi-consumer-group fanout multiplies read load
bottlenecks.trigger: The queue has at least three independent consumer groups reading every record: (1) the persistence writer to KV store, (2) recipient chat servers for WS delivery, (3) the notification service for offline push. Each produce at ~410K/sec peak generates 3x read traffic = ~1.2M consumes/sec. Any consumer group falling behind forces brokers to serve from disk rather than page cache, further amplifying IO.
bottlenecks.symptom: Broker disk read IOPS spike when a consumer group lags; healthy consumer groups see degraded fetch latency due to noisy-neighbor effect; notification delivery lags behind WS delivery during traffic bursts; broker page-cache hit ratio drops below 95%.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run Kafka brokers with sufficient RAM to keep recent ~1 hour of data in page cache (size heap small, leave OS cache large); use tiered storage (Confluent/Pulsar) so older data doesn't pressure hot brokers; isolate the notification consumer group (which tolerates more latency) onto follower-fetch replicas (KIP-392); set consumer fetch.min.bytes=64KB to reduce small-fetch overhead; monitor and auto-scale consumer group replicas independently.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-consumer-group lag dashboards with alert on lag > 30s of production rate; broker disk-read-bytes-per-sec vs network-bytes-out ratio (healthy = near 0 during steady state); page cache hit ratio < 95%; fetch p99 latency > 100ms.

bottlenecks.title: Per-recipient ordering constraint limits partition parallelism
bottlenecks.trigger: Partitioning by recipient_id is required so each user's inbox is an ordered stream (clients depend on monotonic ordering for cur_max_message_id sync). This pins all traffic for a single recipient to one partition and one consumer thread. A celebrity user with many friends or a member of multiple busy groups can receive >1000 msgs/sec into a single partition, exceeding what one consumer thread can forward to WS without head-of-line blocking other recipients on the same partition.
bottlenecks.symptom: Specific users experience delayed message delivery while the fleet looks healthy; consumer group has even partition assignment but skewed throughput per partition; one partition's consumer lags while siblings are caught up; chat servers show uneven queue-to-WS forwarding latency correlated with which recipients they host.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a two-level keying scheme — partition by hash(recipient_id) % N but maintain per-recipient ordering via in-partition key (Kafka preserves order per key within a partition); increase partition count to 2048+ to reduce collision probability for hot recipients; isolate top-1% heavy recipients onto dedicated high-throughput partitions via a custom partitioner; allow consumer to process non-overlapping recipients within a partition in parallel (per-key worker pool) while preserving per-recipient order.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-partition consumer throughput histogram (alert on p99/p50 > 10x); top-N recipient_id by message rate dashboard; per-recipient end-to-end latency (produce-to-WS-push) p99 > 1s; partition lag stddev across the topic.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a queue sitting between chat servers and storage In WhatsApp-style messaging, when Alice sends "hello" to Bob, several things have to happen: the message must be **persisted forever** (chat history), **delivered to Bob's phone** if he's online, and **sent as a push notification** if he isn't. If Alice's chat server tried to do all three synchronously before ACKing her send, her send-path latency would be at the mercy of the slowest of three systems — and any one of them being briefly slow would stall her UI. The sync queue is the "inbox" that decouples the send from the delivery: Alice's server drops one copy per recipient into the queue and is done. Separate consumers (the KV writer, Bob's chat server, the notification service) each pull from the queue at their own pace. ## What breaks without it Without the queue, Alice's chat server would have to directly talk to Bob's chat server (wherever ZooKeeper placed him), *and* write to HBase, *and* call APNs — all before replying to Alice. If Bob's chat server is draining for a deploy, Alice's send hangs. If HBase has a slow region server, every sender feels it. Operators would see message send p99 tracking the worst of three dependencies; users would see spinning "sending…" indicators during any backend hiccup. ## The number Peak is **~70K messages/sec**, and for small groups each send fans out up to 100 copies — so the queue absorbs up to ~7M writes/sec in worst case. Partitioning by `recipient_id` means Bob's inbox is one ordered stream he can replay from on reconnect, which is exactly what multi-device sync needs. ## Trade-off One extra hop (a few ms) and at-least-once semantics (consumers must dedupe by `message_id`) in exchange for send-path latency that doesn't depend on any single downstream.

store.name: Message KV Store
store.summary: Key-value store for chat history. Book recommends HBase (Messenger) or Cassandra (Discord).

sections.heading: Why KV, not relational (book §Storage)
sections.body:
Book's explicit reasons:
- Easy horizontal scaling
- Very low latency
- Relational DBs 'do not handle long tail of data well. When the indexes grow large, random access is expensive.'
- 'Both Facebook messenger and Discord use key-value stores.' — Messenger: HBase; Discord: Cassandra.

sections.heading: 1-on-1 schema (book Figure 12-9)
sections.body:
```
TABLE messages_1on1 message_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY (Snowflake or local seq) sender_id BIGINT recipient_id BIGINT content TEXT created_at TIMESTAMP
```
Primary key = message_id. Book: 'cannot rely on created_at to decide the message sequence because two messages can be created at the same time.'

sections.heading: Group chat schema (book Figure 12-10)
sections.body:
```
TABLE messages_group channel_id BIGINT (partition key) message_id BIGINT (clustering key) sender_id BIGINT content TEXT created_at TIMESTAMP PRIMARY KEY ((channel_id), message_id)
```
Channel_id is the partition key because 'all queries in a group chat operate in a channel.'

sections.heading: Access patterns
sections.body:
- Recent history (hot): last N messages of a channel — single range scan.
- Random access (search, mentions, jump-to-message): supported via message_id lookup.
- Multi-device sync: client pulls `recipient_id == me AND message_id > cur_max_message_id`.

lost: More ops burden
Slower failover than Cassandra
Eventual consistency by default
Smaller community

bottlenecks.title: Write amplification from per-recipient fanout saturates write path
bottlenecks.trigger: The sync-queue persistence consumer writes one row per message for 1:1 (~63K/sec at peak) but the KV store also absorbs multi-device sync reads and group writes. At 70K peak msgs/sec with groups up to 100 members, if the design chooses to also persist per-recipient copies for inbox semantics, writes inflate 10-100x into the 500K-7M writes/sec range. Even the single-row-per-group variant (design's choice) still pushes ~150 TB/year at 2B msgs/day × 200B, concentrated onto channel_id partitions that skew heavily for active large groups.
bottlenecks.symptom: Hot region servers (HBase) or hot partitions (Cassandra) show >80% CPU and compaction backlogs while others idle; write p99 latency climbs from ~10ms to hundreds of ms; consumer lag on the persistence consumer group grows; messages appear in clients (pushed via WS) before they are durably stored, creating a window where a KV store outage loses in-flight messages.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Partition messages_group by (channel_id, bucket=message_id/10000) to split hot channels across multiple partitions while preserving range-scan locality; enable Cassandra's LeveledCompactionStrategy on the messages tables to keep read amplification bounded under heavy writes; batch INSERTs from the persistence consumer (50-100 rows/batch) with async acks; pre-split HBase regions by channel_id hash to avoid initial hotspot; run a dedicated write-heavy cluster separate from read replicas serving history pulls.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-partition write QPS skew dashboard (alert if max/mean > 5x); Cassandra pending compactions > 100 or HBase compaction queue > 50; write p99 latency > 50ms sustained for 2min; persistence consumer lag > 30s of production rate; top-N channel_id by write rate to catch hot groups.

bottlenecks.title: Multi-device sync read storm hits cold partitions
bottlenecks.trigger: On reconnect/foreground, each device issues range reads of form `WHERE recipient_id == me AND message_id > cur_max_message_id`. At 50M DAU with 2-3 devices each and correlated morning wake-up, this produces 5-10M read req/min bursts. Users returning after hours or days trigger deep range scans into cold SSTables/HFiles that bypass the page cache, and the 150 TB/year dataset ensures most random-access reads miss cache entirely.
bottlenecks.symptom: KV store read p99 spikes to seconds during regional wake-up hours while p50 looks fine; disk IOPS pinned on specific nodes holding cold data; client-side time-to-interactive on app foreground degrades to 5-10s; cascading backpressure into the API tier as sync endpoints queue up.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Front the KV store with a Redis-backed recent-inbox cache (last 1-24 hours per user) so 90%+ of sync pulls never touch the KV store; enforce server-side pagination (50 messages/page max) with cursor-based continuation so deep-history fetches are lazy-loaded on scroll; use Cassandra row cache or HBase BlockCache tuned for the hot recent-message range; shard reads across replicas (Cassandra LOCAL_ONE consistency for sync pulls is acceptable since cur_max_message_id provides idempotency); co-locate the recent-inbox cache with chat servers by region.
bottlenecks.detection: Cache hit ratio on recent-inbox cache (alert < 90%); distribution of messages-per-sync-request (alert p99 > 500); KV store read latency p99 broken down by key-range-age (recent vs >1day old); block cache hit ratio on the KV store itself < 80%; correlation between regional wake-up hours and read latency spikes.

bottlenecks.title: Unbounded retention forces cost and operational scaling crisis
bottlenecks.trigger: Book states chat history retained forever. At 2B msgs/day × ~200B/msg = ~400 GB/day raw, ~150 TB/year, ~1.5 PB over a decade before replication factor (3x for Cassandra = 4.5 PB on disk). Bloom filters, index overhead, and SSTable compaction working-set grow linearly; every new node added for write throughput also inherits the full historical read responsibility.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cluster node count grows indefinitely even when traffic is flat; per-node repair/compaction cycles stretch from hours to days, hurting availability during streaming; bootstrap time for a new node climbs past 24 hours making fleet scaling painful; storage cost per DAU trends up year-over-year; JVM heap pressure from bloom filters on huge SSTables.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tiered storage: keep last 90 days on hot NVMe nodes (Cassandra with SSD, HBase HDFS on SSD tier) and migrate older SSTables to cold object storage (S3 via Cassandra tiered storage or HBase Medium Object Storage); use TimeWindowCompactionStrategy keyed on message_id timestamp bits so old data compacts into immutable daily windows that never re-compact; offer per-user retention settings (e.g. 1 year default, unlimited for paid tier) to bound the growth; run a separate archive cluster (lower replication factor, cheaper hardware) for cold reads.
bottlenecks.detection: Track per-node storage utilization and growth rate (alert projected time-to-full < 90 days); bootstrap/repair duration trending; compaction hours/day ratio (alert > 25%); bloom filter heap usage > 30% of JVM heap; cost-per-GB-per-month dashboard with YoY trend.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a KV store holds chat history for WhatsApp For a messaging system retaining chat history **forever** across 50M daily users, storage is the component that has to absorb the most relentless write load in the design — every single message ever sent, from every user, forever. A relational database buckles here for a specific reason the book calls out: as the index grows into the billions of rows, random access (jumping to a specific message, or pulling a user's history after reconnect) gets expensive because B-tree indexes don't handle that "long tail" well. A KV store like HBase or Cassandra keeps writes cheap (append to a log-structured file) and makes range scans within a single partition — e.g. "the last 50 messages in this channel" — a sequential disk read. That's exactly the access pattern chat needs. ## What happens without it If you tried to store chat history in the same relational DB as user profiles, writes would dominate the workload and crowd out profile reads. Operators would see the DB's write-ahead log saturate, replication lag climb, and p99 latency spike across *every* feature — login, friend list, group membership — because they all share the same primary. Users would experience "message sending..." spinners during peak hours and slow app startup as profile queries queue behind message writes. ## The number The design estimates **2B messages/day × 200 bytes × 365 days ≈ 150 TB/year**, growing forever. No single relational primary handles that; you need horizontal partitioning from day one. Cassandra shards by `channel_id` so each group's messages live together on one node — a 50-message history fetch is one partition read, not a scatter-gather across 200 shards. ## Trade-off You give up rich SQL queries (no easy "find all messages mentioning X across all channels") in exchange for linear write scaling and predictable read latency on the one access pattern that actually matters: reading a channel's recent history.

userdb.name: User / Profile DB (relational)
userdb.summary: Stores user profile, settings, friends list, group membership. Book: generic data → relational DB with replication + sharding.

sections.heading: Role (book §Storage)
sections.body:
Book distinguishes two data types:
1. Generic data — user profile, settings, friends list → 'stored in robust and reliable relational databases. Replication and sharding are common techniques.'
2. Chat history → KV store (separate component).

sections.heading: Why keep them separate
sections.body: Access patterns are different: profile is read-mostly with complex joins (friends-of-friends); chat is write-heavy append with simple range scans. One DB can't be optimal for both.

sections.heading: Schema sketch
sections.body:
```
TABLE users (user_id PK, username, email, created_at,...)
TABLE friends (user_id, friend_id, state, PRIMARY KEY (user_id, friend_id))
TABLE groups (channel_id PK, name, created_at, owner_id)
TABLE group_members (channel_id, user_id, role, PRIMARY KEY (channel_id, user_id))
```

lost: Cross-shard queries (friend-of-friend) need app-level fanout
Vertical scaling limits at very large social graphs

bottlenecks.title: group_members lookup hot path on every group send
bottlenecks.trigger: Every group SEND resolves channel_id → member list before fanout. At 70K peak msgs/sec, if ~30% are group messages, that's ~21K group_members reads/sec against the userdb. Sharded by user_id means group_members (keyed by channel_id) either lives on a separate shard scheme or forces scatter-gather. Viral ~100-member groups concentrate reads onto single channel_id rows, creating hot partitions well beyond the 2000-concurrency budget per replica.
bottlenecks.symptom: Group send p99 latency climbs from ~10ms to hundreds of ms; specific DB shards hit 80%+ CPU while others idle; chat servers block on group_members lookups and back up the WS event loop; 1:1 sends on the same chat server also slow due to shared connection pool saturation.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cache group_members in Redis keyed by channel_id with 60–300s TTL, invalidate on membership change via write-through; denormalize member list into the groups row to avoid join; co-locate cache at chat-server tier so group fanout never round-trips to userdb; consider moving group_members out of the relational DB into a dedicated KV store sharded by channel_id.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard QPS and CPU dashboards with skew alert (max/mean > 3x); Redis group_members cache hit ratio (alert < 95%); p99 latency of group_members SELECT > 20ms; top-N channel_id by lookup rate to catch viral groups.

bottlenecks.title: Login bcrypt + userdb SELECT storm during reconnect waves
bottlenecks.trigger: A chat-server zone failure releases millions of clients that fall through to /login if refresh tokens are expired. Each login does a SELECT by username plus a bcrypt verify (~50–100ms CPU). At the configured 2000 concurrency per userdb replica and ~16–50K logins/sec during a herd, the users table's username index hotspot combined with API-tier bcrypt saturation pins the userdb connection pool.
bottlenecks.symptom: Login p99 climbs from ~20ms to multi-second; userdb connection pool exhausted, queuing at API tier; replication lag on read replicas grows; unrelated profile/friends reads also slow because they share pool and replicas; cascading failures into chat reconnect because users can't complete login.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Issue long-lived refresh tokens backed by Redis so reconnects skip the userdb SELECT entirely; rate-limit /login per user_id and per IP (5/min); separate read replicas for the login path from the profile/friends path; use read replicas with LOCAL_ONE-equivalent consistency for username lookups; pre-warm connection pools and cap pool size per API replica to prevent thundering.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on /login QPS > 3x 1-hour baseline; userdb connection pool wait time > 50ms; per-replica CPU > 70%; ratio of /login vs /token/refresh (refresh should dominate >10:1); slow query log for SELECT users WHERE username > 20ms.

bottlenecks.title: Cross-shard friends/friend-of-friend queries fan out expensively
bottlenecks.trigger: Sharding by user_id puts Alice's user row on one shard but her 200 friends scatter across all shards. GET /users/:id/friends expanded with profile preview data (names, avatars) requires either an app-level scatter-gather across N shards or a denormalized copy. At 50M DAU with ~40 app opens/day triggering friends-list refresh, that's ~23K friends-fetch/sec each hitting multiple shards, amplifying effective QPS 10-50x depending on friend count.
bottlenecks.symptom: Friends-list endpoint p99 hundreds of ms even when per-shard p50 is fine; tail latency dominated by slowest shard in scatter-gather; power users (thousands of friends) experience noticeably slower app foreground; shard CPU utilization creeps up uniformly with DAU growth rather than scaling linearly.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cache rendered friends list (with profile preview) in Redis per user_id with 60–300s TTL, invalidate on friend add/remove or profile change; denormalize friend display_name/avatar_url into the friends table row so one shard read returns the full payload without joins; use a dedicated social-graph store (e.g. TAO-style) if friend-of-friend queries become first-class; for power users, paginate friends list and lazy-load beyond first 50.
bottlenecks.detection: p99 latency per shard broken down (alert on scatter-gather tail); friends-cache hit ratio < 90%; distribution of friend_count per request (catch power users); cross-shard query count per friends-fetch (alert p99 > 10 shards touched).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a relational DB for user/profile data in WhatsApp The chat system has two very different kinds of data. Messages are a firehose of short, append-only records that you almost never update — perfect for a KV store. But **user accounts, friend lists, and group membership** look nothing like that: they have structured relationships (Alice is friends with Bob, Bob is in groups 77 and 102, group 77 has members {Alice, Bob, Carol}), they get read constantly during login and every group send, and they need strong consistency (when you remove someone from a group, they should *actually* stop receiving messages). That's exactly what relational databases are good at — indexed lookups by username, joins across `users`/`friends`/`group_members`, and transactional updates when membership changes. ## What breaks without it Without a separate profile DB, you'd be forced to cram account data into the message KV store. Login would become painful — KV stores don't have secondary indexes on `username`, so authenticating "alice" means either a full scan or building your own index table by hand. Group sends would stall because resolving `channel_id → member list` no longer has a clean join. Operators would see login latency spike and group fanout slow down; users would see "can't sign in" errors and delayed group messages. ## The number At 50M DAU with ~40 app opens/day, friends-list and group-membership reads run around **23K reads/sec** fleet-wide — and every one of the ~70K peak messages/sec that's a group send also needs a `group_members` lookup. A relational DB with read replicas handles that indexed-lookup workload cheaply; doing the same in the KV store would mean hand-rolling indexes for every access pattern. ## Trade-off The designer accepted running two storage systems (relational + KV) instead of one, because no single database is optimal for both read-heavy joined profile data and write-heavy append-only message history.

notif.name: Notification Servers
notif.summary: Third-party integration: sends APNs/FCM push notifications to offline recipients. Book's only third-party integration.

sections.heading: When to push (book §1-on-1 chat flow step 5b)
sections.body: Only when recipient has no live WebSocket (presence shows offline). Book calls out push notification as 'crucial' for offline delivery — it is the reason offline users see messages immediately on wake.

sections.heading: Rate limiting
sections.body: Per-recipient token bucket to avoid notification flooding in busy group chats; collapse bursts into 'N new messages'.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- APNs/FCM throttling — backoff and queue; retry later.
- Dead token → mark device invalid after N consecutive failures.

bottlenecks.title: APNs/FCM provider throttling during group-chat notification storms
bottlenecks.trigger: Group sends fan out up to 100 recipients (design's max group size). If even 20% of ~70K peak msgs/sec are group messages averaging 50 offline recipients, notifier must issue ~700K APNs/FCM pushes/sec. APNs HTTP/2 caps ~1000 concurrent streams per connection and throttles aggressively on per-topic burst; FCM enforces per-project QPS quotas (typically 600K/min baseline). Bursts from viral groups or coordinated broadcast events exceed these ceilings in seconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: APNs returns 429/TooManyRequests or closes streams with GOAWAY; FCM returns QUOTA_EXCEEDED; notification consumer lag on the inbox queue grows to minutes; offline users see 'delayed 5 min' push notifications or none at all until they open the app; on-call sees error-rate alerts on APNs client while WS delivery looks healthy.
