bottlenecks.mitigation: Per-recipient token-bucket collapse: if >3 messages queued for the same user within 10s, coalesce into a single 'N new messages in <group>' notification (book's rate-limit guidance); maintain a pool of HTTP/2 connections to APNs (20-50 per notifier pod) to multiply concurrent stream budget; implement exponential backoff with jitter on 429 with retry queue sized to absorb 5-min bursts; pre-negotiate higher FCM quotas and shard across multiple FCM projects; deprioritize group notifications vs 1:1 when throttled.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on APNs/FCM 429 rate > 0.5% of sends over 1min; notification consumer lag > 30s of production rate; per-user push-send rate histogram (p99 > 10/min indicates coalescing failed); dashboard of outbound HTTP/2 GOAWAY frames per minute; track end-to-end offline-send-to-device-wake latency p99 (alert > 10s).

bottlenecks.title: Dead-token accumulation inflates push volume and provider error rates
bottlenecks.trigger: At 50M DAU with 2-3 devices each (~125M device tokens) and typical ~20%/year app-uninstall or token-invalidation churn, the notifier holds ~25M stale tokens at steady state if not aggressively reaped. Every push to a dead token wastes an APNs/FCM call and returns an InvalidRegistration/Unregistered error; at configured 0.005 failure rate against ~700K pushes/sec peak that's ~3.5K errors/sec, but without cleanup the stale-token ratio compounds over months toward 10-20% of outbound volume.
bottlenecks.symptom: APNs/FCM error rate creeps up over weeks without any code change; provider reputation score degrades and delivery priority drops (especially APNs per-topic throttling); notifier CPU/bandwidth wasted on guaranteed failures; users who reinstalled the app complain they aren't getting notifications because the new token wasn't registered while old tokens still exist for them.
bottlenecks.mitigation: On InvalidRegistration/Unregistered/BadDeviceToken responses, immediately mark token as dead in pn_db (don't wait for N consecutive failures for these deterministic error codes); run a daily sweep that reaps tokens with any terminal error flag; enforce token refresh on every app foreground via API so re-installs immediately replace old tokens; keep at most 3 active tokens per user and LRU-evict the rest; use APNs feedback-style endpoint (now via unregistered response codes) as authoritative.
bottlenecks.detection: Track ratio of InvalidRegistration responses over total sends (alert > 2%); dashboard active-tokens-per-user distribution (alert if p99 > 5); weekly trend of stale-token reap counts; per-user push success ratio broken down by device_id.

bottlenecks.title: Busy group chats trigger notification flooding and user opt-out
bottlenecks.trigger: A 100-member group with 30 active participants can produce 100+ messages in a minute. For each of the ~70 offline members, that's 100 push notifications in 60 seconds from a single group. Without coalescing, a single busy group saturates a user's lock screen and breaches platform UX expectations; at 50M DAU even 1% of users in such groups = 500K users getting notification-spammed per event.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users disable notifications for the app entirely (measurable drop in opt-in rate); app-store reviews complain of 'too many notifications'; platform OS (iOS Focus modes, Android notification channels) auto-suppresses the app's notifications; notifier bandwidth dominated by a small number of hot groups.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Per-(user, channel_id) token bucket: max 1 push per 5s per group chat, coalesce intermediate messages into a single 'N new messages from <group>' summary on the next tick (book's explicit rate-limit guidance); respect user's per-channel mute/notification-level settings server-side before calling APNs/FCM; for groups above a threshold of activity, switch automatically to digest-mode notifications (one every 2 minutes); leverage APNs collapse-id and FCM collapse_key so the device only renders the latest.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-user push-rate histogram (alert if p99 > 20/hour from a single channel); track notification opt-out rate per cohort over time; sample top-N channel_id by notifications-sent-per-minute dashboard; platform-reported notification-delivery-to-display ratio (APNs/FCM analytics) to detect OS-level suppression.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why notification servers are in the WhatsApp design The problem statement explicitly lists "push notifications" as a required feature — and for a good reason. A chat server can only deliver a message in real time if the recipient has a live WebSocket open. But most of your friends, most of the time, don't have the app open. Their phone is in their pocket, screen off, WhatsApp backgrounded by the OS to save battery. There is no WebSocket to push to. The only way to wake that phone is through Apple's APNs or Google's FCM — services the OS itself listens to even when your app is asleep. The notification servers are the bridge between the chat system's internal message queue and those third-party gateways. ## What happens without it If you ripped this tier out, offline users would only learn about new messages the next time they manually opened the app. A message sent to Bob at 9 AM would sit in the KV store until 3 PM when he happens to check — his phone never buzzes. Operators would see the message was successfully stored and the presence service correctly marked Bob offline; nothing looks broken in the logs. But users would churn, because a messaging app that doesn't notify you of messages is worse than SMS. ## The number At 50M DAU with ~20% concurrently online, that leaves **~40M users offline at any moment**. With peak traffic of ~70K messages/sec, and group fanout up to 100 recipients, a busy hour could require hundreds of thousands of APNs/FCM pushes per second — which is why notification is its own scaled tier, not a side-task on the chat server. The trade-off: you now depend on Apple and Google as critical third parties, with their own throttling and failure modes.

blob.name: Media Blob Store (extension)
blob.summary: Object storage for photos / videos / voice — book flags this as an extension beyond the text-only base scope.

sections.heading: Why direct upload
sections.body: Routing media through chat servers wastes bandwidth. Client POSTs to signed S3/GCS URL; message body only carries the blob ref.

sections.heading: Book's note
sections.body: Book lists 'media files such as photos and videos' as a post-interview talking point alongside compression, cloud storage, and thumbnails. Not in the base design.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: - S3 partial outage → client retries with exponential backoff; message is marked 'sending' until media settles.

gained: Tight integration with GCP media pipeline
lost: Cross-cloud egress fees

bottlenecks.title: Egress bandwidth and cost explosion from group media fanout
bottlenecks.trigger: A photo/video sent to a 100-member group is uploaded once but downloaded up to 100 times via signed GET URLs. At 50M DAU, if even 5% of ~70K peak msgs/sec carry media averaging 500KB (photos) to 5MB (videos), with 30% being group sends averaging 50 recipients, peak egress reaches 10-50 GB/sec (~80-400 Gbps). S3/GCS egress at $0.05-0.09/GB translates to millions of dollars/month; bandwidth also competes with upload traffic on the same buckets.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cloud bill spikes dominated by egress line item; media downloads slow during peak hours as bucket request-rate quotas throttle (S3 default 5,500 GET/sec per prefix); users on cellular networks see 'loading image...' for tens of seconds; CDN origin-fetch traffic saturates during viral media events.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Front the blob store with a CDN (CloudFront/Cloud CDN) so each media object is fetched once from origin and cached at edge — cuts origin egress by 10-100x and moves bytes closer to users; generate signed CDN URLs instead of raw S3 URLs; shard uploads across many prefixes (e.g. hash-prefixed keys) to escape S3 per-prefix rate limits; generate and serve thumbnails/transcoded variants (360p/720p) so most views hit smaller objects; set aggressive Cache-Control (immutable, 1yr) since blob_refs are content-addressed.
bottlenecks.detection: Dashboard egress GB/sec per bucket with alert > 80% of provisioned limit; S3 5xx SlowDown response rate > 0.1%; CDN cache hit ratio (alert < 90%); per-object fetch-count distribution (catch viral media); monthly egress cost trend vs DAU growth.

bottlenecks.title: Signed URL abuse and token leakage enabling unauthorized access
bottlenecks.trigger: Signed upload/download URLs embed time-bounded credentials valid for minutes to hours. At ~70K msgs/sec with media traffic, millions of signed URLs are minted per hour. URLs leak via client logs, shared screenshots, browser history, or accidental forwarding. A URL for a private photo sent to one recipient can be replayed by anyone who obtains it, bypassing WhatsApp's auth entirely since blob store has no knowledge of channel membership.
bottlenecks.symptom: Security incident reports of media accessed by non-members; forensic logs show downloads from IPs/regions inconsistent with the intended recipient; bug-bounty reports of URL-sharing exploits; auditors flag that media access lacks per-fetch authorization; no server-side way to revoke a leaked URL before its TTL expires.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Keep signed URL TTLs short (5-15 min for downloads, 60 min for uploads) to shrink leak window; require a per-request auth token header validated by a lightweight API proxy (Lambda@Edge or CloudFront signed cookies + Function) that checks channel membership before serving; encrypt media client-side with per-message keys so leaked URLs return ciphertext useless without the key (true E2E); log every GET with user_id + IP and alert on anomalous access patterns; rotate signing keys periodically.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on signed-URL reuse rate > 1 fetch per URL (should be ~1:1 with recipient count); geo-IP mismatch between uploader's region and downloader's region beyond expected friend-graph distribution; per-object fetch count exceeding group-member count by >2x; audit-log ingestion of 4xx auth failures on the API proxy.

bottlenecks.title: Upload failures leave 'sending...' messages stuck with no reconciliation
bottlenecks.trigger: Client uploads directly to S3/GCS, then sends the SEND envelope referencing blob_ref. Between these two steps, the client may crash, lose network, or succeed the upload but fail to deliver the SEND (the 0.001 failure rate on blob × ~0.0005 on chat path × millions of media sends/day = thousands of orphan cases/day). Conversely, the SEND may arrive but the upload partially failed (S3 multipart abort), leaving recipients with a broken blob_ref.
bottlenecks.symptom: Recipients see 'image unavailable' or infinite loading spinners for media that supposedly sent successfully; sender's UI shows message delivered but recipient's GET returns 404/403; orphan objects accumulate in the blob store (pay for storage of unreferenced blobs); support tickets about 'my photo didn't send' despite sender seeing a checkmark.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Two-phase commit via blob-ref reservation: client requests a blob_ref before upload; API records it in a pending-uploads table with 24h TTL; client uploads, then confirms via SEND; a background reaper deletes unreferenced reservations after TTL. Client-side: only mark message as 'sent' after both upload 200 AND SEND ACK; retry SEND with idempotent client_msg_id until ACK received; on recipient side, if blob_ref GET returns 404 within first 60s, retry with backoff before showing error. Use S3 multipart with explicit completion + integrity check (Content-MD5).
bottlenecks.detection: Metric for orphan-blob ratio (objects uploaded but never referenced by a delivered message) alert > 0.5%; client-side send-failure telemetry where upload succeeded but SEND failed; recipient-side blob GET 404 rate on first-view > 0.1%; daily reaper run reporting reclaimed storage bytes (trending up indicates rising failure rate).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the blob store sits outside the main message path WhatsApp-style chat is really two workloads glued together. Text messages are *tiny* — a few hundred bytes — and flow through chat servers, a queue, and a KV store that are all tuned for small, fast, high-frequency writes. Photos and videos are the opposite: a single 5 MB video is bigger than 25,000 text messages combined. If you tried to push that video through the same WebSocket and the same Kafka-style sync queue that handle \"hello,\" you'd clog the chat server's memory, blow out queue partition sizes, and make the KV store's 200-byte row model a lie. The blob store exists so the big bytes take a completely different path — the client uploads directly to S3/GCS, and the message envelope that flows through chat only carries a tiny reference string like `blob_ref: "abc123"`. ## What breaks without it If media went through chat servers, a few users sending videos during peak hour would starve everyone else's text messages — send-path p99 would spike, WebSocket buffers would back up, and operators would see chat server memory climb until OOM kills the process, disconnecting 50,000 users at once. Meanwhile the KV store, sized for 200 B/row, would suddenly have multi-MB rows destroying its compaction math. ## The number The design estimates ~70K peak messages/sec. If even 5% carry a 500 KB photo, that's 70,000 × 0.05 × 500 KB = **1.75 GB/sec** of media bytes. Routing that through 200 chat servers means ~70 Mbps per server *just for media* — on top of text and WebSocket overhead. Uploading directly to blob storage drops that to near zero on the chat tier. The trade-off: you now depend on a third storage system and must manage signed URLs, but the chat path stays lean and predictable.

operations.title: Login + service discovery (pick best chat server)
operations.name: Login + service discovery (pick best chat server)
operations.description: Book Figure 12-11. User logs in via API servers; ZooKeeper picks the best chat server; client opens WebSocket to it.

steps.title: User opens the app and submits credentials
steps.action: Client POSTs username/password (or refresh token) over plain HTTPS to the API tier.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json {"username": "alice", "password": "..."}

steps.title: LB routes login to API tier
steps.action: Round-robin to any healthy API replica — signup/login are fully stateless.

steps.title: API authenticates against user DB
steps.action: API server looks up the user row, verifies hashed password, and issues a session token.
steps.codeOrCommand:
row = userdb.query("SELECT id, pw_hash FROM users WHERE username=?", username)
if not bcrypt.verify(password, row.pw_hash): return 401
token = jwt.sign({"user_id": row.id})

steps.title: User DB returns user row
steps.action: Single indexed lookup by username; Postgres returns in a few ms.

steps.title: API asks service discovery for best chat server
steps.action: Book step: 'service discovery finds the best chat server for User A'. Criteria: geographic proximity, current load, health.
steps.codeOrCommand: best = zk.pick_chat_server(user_id=4201, geo="US-WEST")

steps.title: ZooKeeper returns chat-server-2
steps.action: ZooKeeper inspects its registered chat-server ephemeral znodes, filters healthy ones, and picks the best by load + geo.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# conceptual
alive = [c for c in chat_servers if c.healthy]
ranked = sorted(alive, key=lambda c: (c.geo_dist(user), c.load))
return ranked[0] # chat-server-2

tradeoffs.rationale: WebSocket gives bidirectional server push at ~10 KB per idle connection; long-polling at 10M users would mean 2M empty GETs/sec. The cost is connection affinity, which complicates rolling deploys.
A chat is a time-ordered append log per channel — exactly the workload Cassandra is best at. RDBMS would need cross-shard joins once channels spread across hosts.
Clients need the least-loaded chat server and must re-resolve after crashes. DNS TTLs are too coarse; ZooKeeper gives sub-second reroute. The cost is another stateful dependency to operate.

tradeoffs.chosen: Durable per-user inbox queue plus APNs/FCM wake
tradeoffs.rationale: Storing the message in an inbox lets reconnecting devices drain at their own pace; APNs/FCM pushes wake background apps without running our own mobile daemon. The tradeoff is dual-write complexity between the message log and the inbox.

tradeoffs.chosen: Heartbeat every 5 s with 30 s offline threshold
tradeoffs.rationale: Short enough to feel live, long enough to tolerate brief tunnels and NAT rebinds. Shorter intervals drain mobile batteries; longer intervals make 'online' dots lie.
